title: Leveraging the Power of Conversations: Optimal Key Term Selection in Conversational Contextual Bandits

problem.claim: Conversational contextual bandits seek to improve preference learning by balancing exploitation and exploration in conversational recommender systems.

gap.claim: Existing methods insufficiently explore user preferences and use deterministic conversation initiation rules that can cause unnecessary interactions or missed opportunities under uncertainty.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes CLiSK, CLiME, and CLiSK-ME for key-term selection and adaptive conversation initiation in conversational contextual bandits.
The three algorithms are theoretically shown to achieve a regret upper bound of O(√dTlogT), and a matching lower bound Ω(√dT) is provided for conversational bandits.
The proposed approaches are evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe CLiSK, CLiME, and CLiSK-ME as novel algorithms.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the approaches achieve at least a 14.6% improvement in cumulative regret on synthetic and real-world datasets.
The authors report that the algorithms are nearly minimax optimal based on the stated upper and lower bounds.

narrative_sequence.summary: Conversational recommenders use key terms and feedback to elicit preferences for personalized recommendations.
Conversational contextual bandits balance exploitation and exploration, but existing approaches face effectiveness limitations.
Current methods inadequately explore preferences and rely on deterministic conversation initiation that can be inefficient or miss uncertainty-driven opportunities.
The paper introduces three algorithms combining smoothed key-term contexts with adaptive conversation initiation.
The authors report theoretical regret guarantees and improved cumulative regret in synthetic and real-world evaluations.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the synthetic and real-world datasets.
The abstract does not specify baselines, evaluation settings, or statistical details.
The abstract does not state the assumptions underlying the theoretical bounds.
